slides.title: Spoken Tutorial on Introduction to Building with AI
slides.narration: Welcome to this Spoken Tutorial on Introduction to Building with AI.

slides.title: Learning Objectives
slides.narration:
In this tutorial, you will learn to,

• Define what an **API** is.
• Explain the purpose of an **API** key.
• Identify components of an **API** request.

slides.title: System Requirements
slides.narration: Here I am using a browser on a computer or mobile.

slides.title: Pre-requisite
slides.narration: To follow this tutorial, you should have completed Module 2: Introduction to Prompting.

slides.title: What is an API? The Restaurant Waiter
slides.narration:
Have you ever wondered how apps talk to powerful **AI** models?
They use something called an **API**.
**API** stands for **Application Programming Interface**.
Think of an **API** like a restaurant waiter.
You give your order to the waiter.
The waiter takes your order to the kitchen.
The kitchen prepares your food.
Similarly, your application gives instructions to the **API**.
The **API** delivers these instructions to an **AI** model.
The **AI** model processes them and sends back a response.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration showing a restaurant waiter taking an order from a customer (application), carrying it to the kitchen (AI model), and bringing back food (response).

slides.title: What is an API Key? Your Restaurant ID Card
slides.narration:
How does the **AI** model know who is sending the request?
This is where an **API key** comes in.
An **API key** is a secret password.
It identifies you as an authorized user.
Imagine it like your restaurant ID card.
This card proves you are allowed to order food.
Similarly, your **API key** authenticates your application.
It ensures only authorized users access the **AI** model.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration of a person showing an ID card to gain access, representing authentication, with a lock icon.

slides.title: Real-Life Example: Searching in a Grocery App
slides.narration:
Let's see how this works in real life.
Open any grocery app on your phone.
Tap the search bar at the top.
Type 'tomato' and press search.
Behind the scenes, the app sends a request to the **API**.
The **API** searches for all matching products.
The server sends back a list of results.
You now see all tomato products on your screen.
This is an **API** in action!
slides.image_prompt: Screen close-up: user typing 'tomato' into the search bar of a grocery app on a smartphone.

slides.title: What is an API Request? Placing Your Order
slides.narration:
Now that we know about **API**s and **API key**s, what about the actual communication?
This communication is called an **API request**.
An **API request** is like placing your order at the restaurant.
It includes your **API key** for authentication.
It also contains your instructions for the **AI** model.
These instructions are often called a **prompt**.
So, you send a structured **API request**.
This request tells the **AI** model what to do.
It's how you ask the **AI** model for a specific task.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration showing a person (application) handing an order slip (API request) to a waiter, with a small key icon on the slip for authentication and text 'prompt' on the order.

slides.title: Summary
slides.narration:
Let us summarize what we learned.
We defined **API**s as messengers.
We understood **API key**s as identification.
We learned about **API request**s as structured orders to **AI** models.

slides.title: Assignment
slides.narration:
Now as an assignment,
Identify other real-life applications using **API**s.
Consider what information their **API request**s might include.
Compare the results.
